title: Predictive Quota Smoothing — Idea Pad
body:
Context:

This is a user-facing and infra-facing sketch about smoothing hard per-account quotas / rate limits so product UX is less brittle during traffic spikes and billing cycles. The idea: predict short-term demand and temporarily smooth credits/burst headroom to avoid sharp rejections, while preserving long-term economic guards (monthly caps, committed capacity).

Why:
- Many customers build user experiences that rely on predictable API availability. Abrupt quota exhaustion triggers poor UX and unnecessary support tickets.
- We sell committed capacity and per-token usage; we need to protect backplane cost while reducing false-positive throttles.
- Existing approaches are conservative static caps or coarse burst tokens; both either block too early or let customers spike cost unexpectedly.

Goals (product + metrics):
- Reduce customer-visible rejection rate during short surges by 40% for mid-tier customers (30d trial).
- Keep 95th percentile monthly cost exposure within 10% of baseline for any smoothing window (protect finance).
- Provide observability per-account for when smoothing was applied and why.

Key user stories:
- As an app developer, I want requests to be accepted during a sudden 2–5 minute user-driven spike (e.g., onboarding surge), so my product flow doesn't break.
- As a platform engineer, I want to limit the total additional cost from smoothing per account in a billing cycle, and detect accounts that repeatedly game smoothing.
- As an account owner (enterprise), I want the option to opt out of smoothing for compliance/forecasting reasons.

High-level design sketch:
1) Short-term demand predictor:
   - Lightweight model per account (or tiered by profile) predicting expected requests/minute over the next N minutes. Features: recent request rate, rolling device-level signals (if available), day-of-week/hour-of-day, history of burst events, campaign flags (if customer provides), region.
   - Default looks: simple exponential smoothing + anomaly detection; optional ML model for high volume accounts.

2) Smoothing policy engine:
   - Each account has a smoothing budget (credits) per billing window. Budget consumes when we serve above nominal quota. Budget replenishes slowly or via purchased burst packs.
   - Policy decisions: allow, degrade (lower fidelity model/quantize), queue, or reject. Decision uses predicted short-term demand + remaining smoothing credits + global capacity footprint.

3) Degradation ladder (cost control):
   - Level 0: full quality, charged normally, consumes smoothing credits.
   - Level 1: aggressive batching/longer response window (trade latency for tokens). Preferred for hosted API clients that can accept streaming delay.
   - Level 2: lower-fidelity model or quantized variant (less cost), small chance of quality regressions.
   - Level 3: reject when budget exhausted or event is sustained (not a spike).

Operational considerations:
- Telemetry: emit smoothing-applied events, reason codes, pre/post latency and token deltas. Provide a dashboard showing smoothing by account and by route.
- Safety: hard global circuit breakers to avoid cross-account capacity collapse.
- Billing: generate an audit trail so CSMs can explain an unexpected surcharge (show smoothing windows + tokens served).

Experiment plan (MVP):
- Phase A (2 weeks): server-side simulation using past 90d traffic to estimate how often smoothing would have prevented rejects and the cost delta. Produce a heatmap of candidate accounts.
- Phase B (4–6 weeks): closed beta with 10 SMB customers and internal sandbox. Expose a flag for 'lenient-mode' where we allow smoothing but notify account owner via usage logs. Track KPIs: reject rate, monthly cost delta, customer satisfaction.
- Phase C: gradual rollout with opt-in and admin settings (max smoothing credit per 24h).

Acceptance criteria (MVP):
- Simulation shows >=30% reduction in short-spike rejects with <=15% cost delta for selected cohort.
- Observability surface implemented (per-account logs + dashboard).
- Customer opt-out and billing audit log present.

Open questions / risks:
- Abuse: accounts intentionally creating micro-bursts to consume others' smoothing? How to detect and penalize?
- Predictive model cold start: new accounts have little history. Conservative fallback needed.
- Enterprise SLAs: will smoothing be incompatible with some enterprise contracts? Need per-account toggles and clear documentation.
- Legal/Compliance: smoothing can change observed traffic patterns; ensure logs/audit meet retention/compliance needs.

Notes on implementation complexity:
- MVP can be conservative: use rolling averages and simple credit bucket. Defer per-account ML models to second phase.
- Prefer to implement policy engine as part of routing layer so we can pick degradation strategies pre-inference (model variant switch) instead of post-factum.

Next steps / TODOs:
- Run simulation job: historical-sim/JOB-2025-11 (Calvin to pick 10 candidate accounts).
- Draft quick UX note for Console: indicate smoothing active windows and ability to opt-out. (Elio)
- Write an internal RFC with architecture diagram and capacity safeguards.

Longer-term ideas (parking lot):
- Smoothing marketplace: customers can buy daily burst packs that auto-top-up credits.
- Cross-account cooperative smoothing for orgs with multiple sub-accounts.
- Predictive pre-warming where we proactively spin ephemeral capacity when a large campaign is forecasted (paid feature).

If you read this and have a concrete customer case where short-term spikes broke a flow, drop a short note below — I'll prioritize those accounts for closed beta.

Quick notes from sync with Calvin (2026-02-15):
- He saw many rejected requests from onboarding flows that lasted 3–7 minutes; these would map well to a smoothing window of 10 min and small credit cost.
- Finance is willing to tolerate a 10% cost delta for the pilot if we can show improved retention on onboarding flows.

-- Theo
